headline: Mongolia's president says he will resign

sources.title: Mongolia's president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption (AP, via Arab Times)
Mongolia president resigns after graft accusations (AFP, via The Straits Times)
Mongolian president announces resignation after mining inquiry calls (dpa, via Yahoo News)

chunks.text: Mongolia's president said on November 17, 2026, that he would {{step down}} after [[accusations]] of [[corruption]]. Mongolia is a large country with no coast, between Russia and China. The president [[denied]] doing anything wrong, and no court had found him [[guilty]]. He said he would become an [[ordinary citizen]]. No Mongolian president had ever quit [[voluntarily]] before the end of a term in office.

verbs.wrong: To sing at a state dinner
verbs.why: The team captain steps down after ten years. Many company bosses step down when they reach 65. Mongolia's president said he would step down after accusations of corruption.

chunks.text: The claims {{came out}} on November 14. A former mayor of the capital made them. He belongs to a [[rival group]] inside the president's own party. He accused the president of taking 25 million dollars in [[bribes]], secret payments for [[special favors]]. The accusation says a large company {{paid the president off}} to win a [[railroad contract]] in 2019, when he was prime minister. The company denied paying any cash bribes.

verbs.correct: To become known to the public
verbs.wrong: To be paid in gold coins
verbs.why: The truth often comes out after a long time. Secrets come out fast in a small town. The claims against Mongolia's president came out on November 14, 2026.

verbs.correct: To secretly give money for a favor
verbs.wrong: To send someone a bill for work
verbs.why: Some criminals pay off police officers to avoid arrest. Dishonest builders pay off inspectors to pass bad work. The accusation says a large company paid the president off to win a railroad contract.

chunks.text: On November 16, the [[opposition]] Democratic Party, which is not in power, {{called on}} the president to resign. It said [[lawmakers]] could otherwise {{force him out}} through [[impeachment]], a legal process for removing a president. The president {{fired back}} at the claims. "I have never stolen from my people or my state," he said. He promised to work with [[investigators]] as they {{dig into}} the case. A former prime minister from the opposition said the resignation must begin an effort to {{root out}} corruption.

verbs.correct: To ask someone firmly to act
verbs.wrong: To praise someone in a speech
verbs.why: Parents call on the school to make the street safer. Doctors call on the city to clean the air. The Democratic Party called on the president to resign.

verbs.correct: To make someone leave a job
verbs.wrong: To pay someone a lower salary
verbs.why: Angry owners force out a coach after a bad season. Some boards force out a CEO when profits fall. The party said lawmakers could force the president out through impeachment.
People fire back when someone spreads lies about them. Some politicians fire back at bad news stories. The president fired back at the claims and said he had never stolen.

verbs.correct: To study the facts of a case
verbs.wrong: To write the rules for a court
verbs.why: Reporters dig into problems at city hall. Tax officers dig into a company's records. The president promised to work with investigators as they dig into the case.

verbs.correct: To find and remove something bad
verbs.why: Good managers root out waste in their companies. Schools work hard to root out cheating. A former prime minister wants an effort to root out corruption.

chunks.text: The resignation needed parliament's approval to [[take effect]]. A vote was expected later that week. Under Mongolian law, the [[speaker of parliament]], its top officer, {{takes over}} as [[acting president]] after a president leaves. A new election must follow within four months. Earlier in 2026, thousands of young people {{turned out}} in the capital to protest corruption. In January 2021, the president {{gave up}} his job as prime minister. He {{went on to}} win the presidency six months later.

verbs.why: A new nurse takes over when the day shift ends. The vice president takes over when the president is away. Under Mongolian law, the speaker of parliament takes over as acting president after a president leaves.

verbs.wrong: To leave a job for a year
verbs.why: Big crowds turn out for the town parade. Thousands of fans turn out for the final game. Earlier in 2026, thousands of young people turned out in Mongolia's capital to protest corruption.

verbs.correct: To stop having a job or power
verbs.wrong: To earn more money at work
verbs.why: Many parents give up a job to stay home with a baby. Some leaders give up power when they get old. The president gave up his job as prime minister in January 2021.

verbs.correct: To do something next in your life
verbs.wrong: To teach something at a school
verbs.why: Many good students go on to become doctors. Some small-town singers go on to win big prizes. After he left the prime minister's job, he went on to win the presidency.

mainIdea.s: Mongolia's president said he would leave office after being accused of taking bribes tied to a railroad deal. He denied the claims, and parliament was expected to vote on his decision.
mainIdea.why: He said he would step down after the accusations came out. He denied them, and the speaker of parliament takes over after a president leaves.

mainIdea.s: The leader of Mongolia is quitting because he admitted that he accepted secret payments from a big company. Opposition lawmakers now plan to remove him from office with an impeachment vote.
mainIdea.why: Close, but he admitted nothing. He fired back at the claims and said he had never stolen from his people or his state.

mainIdea.s: China and Mongolia have signed an agreement to build a long train line for coal across their border. Officials in both countries expect the work to create many jobs within four years.
mainIdea.why: This is about the president saying he would step down after corruption claims, not a new agreement with China.

lines.text: Did you see the news from Mongolia? The president said he would {{step down}}.
A former mayor of the capital accused him of taking 25 million dollars in bribes.
No, from his own party, but from a rival group. The claims {{came out}} on November 14.
Wow. If he's innocent, that's [[a stab in the back]].
Right. The accusation says a big company {{paid him off}} to win a railroad contract.
It denies paying any cash bribes. The president {{fired back}} too. He said he never stole anything.
He said he wanted to [[clear his name]]. He was also [[under pressure]]. The opposition {{called on}} him to resign, or lawmakers could {{force him out}}.
Sounds like there's a lot of [[bad blood]] in Mongolian politics.
It seems that way. Investigators can {{dig into}} it, and he promised to help them.
So who would run the country?
Parliament had to vote first. Under the law, the speaker {{takes over}} after a president leaves. [[As far as I know]], the election has to happen within four months.
Could this be the end of his career?
Nobody knows. He {{gave up}} the prime minister's job in 2021 and {{went on to}} win the presidency.
Interesting. I want to see what happens next.
